21484949.study_design: multicenter fMRI activation pattern study using PCA-based descriptive clustering

27166430.model_family: support vector machine with graph kernel PCA feature extraction
27166430.clinical_problem: ADHD diagnosis from resting-state fMRI brain networks
27166430.patient_population: children and adolescents with ADHD (118) versus normal controls (98) from the ADHD-200 dataset
27166430.model_description: Resting-state fMRI-derived whole-brain connectivity networks are searched for discriminative subnetworks that differ between ADHD and control groups. A graph kernel principal component analysis extracts features from these subnetworks, and a support vector machine classifies each subject as ADHD or normal control. The method was trained and tested on the ADHD-200 dataset (118 ADHD, 98 controls).
27166430.dataset_size: 118 ADHD patients and 98 normal controls (ADHD-200 dataset)
27166430.headline_result: 94.91% accuracy for ADHD vs. normal control classification, 9.20% higher than prior state-of-the-art methods
27166430.study_design: retrospective classification study using a public dataset

28635541.model_family: one-class support vector machine (OC-SVM) on graph-theory eigenvector centrality features
28635541.clinical_problem: classifying typical versus atypical brain network organization from resting-state fMRI and its relation to psychopathology
28635541.model_description: Eigenvector centrality, a graph-theory measure of node importance, is computed from resting-state fMRI connectivity in children and adolescents. A one-class support vector machine trained on this feature labels each individual's brain network as typical or atypical. Subjects classified as atypical had higher levels of psychopathology.
28635541.headline_result: Subjects with atypical brain network organization had significantly higher psychopathology levels (p < 0.001)

28971013.clinical_problem: predicting response to vagus nerve stimulation from presurgical resting-state fMRI connectivity in children with intractable epilepsy
28971013.patient_population: 21 children (ages 5-21 years) with medically intractable epilepsy undergoing VNS; independent external cohort of 8 children
28971013.model_description: Whole-brain resting-state fMRI connectivity to thalamic regions of interest is measured before vagus nerve stimulation implantation in children with drug-resistant epilepsy. A supervised support vector machine trained on this connectivity classifies patients as responders or non-responders to VNS, and was tested in an independent external cohort. Enhanced thalamic connectivity to the anterior cingulate cortex and left insula was associated with greater treatment benefit.
28971013.headline_result: 86% accuracy on 10-fold cross-validation; 88% accuracy in an independent external validation cohort of 8 children
28971013.study_design: retrospective diagnostic/prognostic accuracy study with external validation

30009990.model_family: L1-norm support vector machine, bi-objective optimization
30009990.patient_population: school-aged children with and without ADHD
30009990.model_description: fMRI-derived features from children are input to an L1-norm support vector machine formulated as a bi-objective optimization that trades off margin of separation against empirical classification error, producing a family of candidate classifiers for ADHD diagnosis. The normal boundary intersection method is used to generate the trade-off curve, avoiding manual tuning of the regularization parameter.

30425750.model_family: machine learning regression algorithm using brain network graph metrics
30425750.clinical_problem: predicting full-scale IQ from resting-state fMRI brain network metrics in children with epilepsy
30425750.patient_population: 24 children with focal epilepsy, ages 8-18 years
30425750.model_description: Resting-state fMRI brain network metrics (clustering coefficient, modularity, path length, global efficiency), computed using either Pearson correlation or mutual information to define connectivity, are input to a machine learning algorithm trained to predict full-scale IQ in children with epilepsy. Mutual-information-based network metrics explained more IQ variance than correlation-based metrics.
30425750.headline_result: Mutual information network metrics explained 49% (95% CI 46-51%) of IQ variance versus 17% (95% CI 13-19%) for Pearson correlation

30440303.clinical_problem: distinguishing treated from untreated adolescent major depressive disorder using anatomical (DTI) connectivity
30440303.patient_population: 52 adolescents with major depressive disorder (37 treated, 15 untreated)
30440303.model_description: Diffusion tensor imaging anatomical connectivity between brain-region pairs and derived network topology measures are used to train a nonlinear support vector machine. The classifier distinguishes adolescents with major depressive disorder who received treatment from those who did not, using features selected by p-value filtering and minimum-redundancy-maximum-relevance, evaluated with leave-one-out cross-validation.

30440968.clinical_problem: identifying anatomical biomarkers distinguishing adolescent major depressive disorder from healthy controls using diffusion weighted imaging
30440968.patient_population: 79 adolescents with and without major depressive disorder
30440968.model_description: Diffusion tensor imaging anatomical connectivity and network topology features are input to a support vector machine trained to distinguish adolescents with major depressive disorder from healthy controls. Features were selected by p-value filtering combined with minimum-redundancy-maximum-relevance, and performance was assessed by leave-one-out cross-validation.

30537564.clinical_problem: classifying emotional condition and age group from task fMRI activation during naturalistic emotion processing
30537564.patient_population: 21 adults and 30 children (mean age 7.75 years) undergoing task fMRI
30537564.model_description: BOLD fMRI activation recorded while children and adults watched movie clips portraying positive, negative, and neutral emotions is used to train multivariate support vector machines. The models classify the emotional condition being viewed and distinguish children from adults within each condition, based on activity in sensory, socio-emotional, and emotion-regulation regions.
30537564.headline_result: 61.44% accuracy classifying emotional condition across all participants; adults vs. children significantly distinguished within each condition (p < 0.05)

30835738.model_family: machine learning regression algorithm on normalized brain network metrics
30835738.clinical_problem: predicting individual IQ from resting-state fMRI brain network architecture in children with epilepsy
30835738.model_description: Brain network graph metrics (clustering coefficient, transitivity, modularity, path length, global efficiency) are computed from resting-state fMRI in children with epilepsy under two normalization strategies. A machine learning algorithm uses only these normalized metrics to predict each patient's IQ, with normalization substantially improving prediction accuracy over non-normalized metrics.
30835738.headline_result: Normalization substantially improved subject-level IQ prediction accuracy versus non-normalized network metrics

30873514.clinical_problem: predicting autism spectrum disorder treatment outcome and classifying autistic versus typically developing children from task fMRI
30873514.patient_population: children with autism spectrum disorder (N=21 for treatment-outcome prediction; N=40 for ASD vs. typical classification)
30873514.model_description: Task-based fMRI data from small pediatric cohorts are used to train recurrent neural networks, aided by ROI-based resampling data augmentation, inclusion of non-imaging variables for subject-specific initialization, and selection of the most generalizable model across multiple training runs. The resulting RNNs predict treatment outcome for children with autism spectrum disorder and classify autistic versus typically developing children from task-fMRI scans.
30873514.dataset_size: 21 children (treatment outcome); 40 children (ASD vs. typical classification)
30873514.study_design: technical development, retrospective small-cohort classification study

30983979.model_family: naive Bayes, random forest, and support vector machine classifiers
30983979.clinical_problem: classifying auditory over-responsivity in children from diffusion tensor imaging and connectome edge-density metrics
30983979.patient_population: 39 boys, ages 8-12 years, with and without auditory over-responsivity
30983979.model_description: Diffusion tensor imaging metrics (fractional anisotropy, mean/radial/axial diffusivity) and derived connectome edge-density maps of white matter tracts are input to naive Bayes, random forest, and support vector machine classifiers. The models were trained and compared to classify boys with versus without auditory over-responsivity, with random forest using edge-density metrics performing best.
30983979.dataset_size: 39 boys, ages 8-12 years (15 with auditory over-responsivity)
30983979.headline_result: Left superior longitudinal fasciculus FA gave AUC 0.756 for AOR prediction (p = 0.008); random forest with edge-density metrics had the highest classification accuracy among tested models

31330239.clinical_problem: distinguishing pediatric bipolar disorder, disruptive mood dysregulation disorder, and healthy controls from diffusion tensor imaging white matter microstructure
31330239.patient_population: 118 youths: 36 with bipolar disorder, 44 with disruptive mood dysregulation disorder, 38 healthy volunteers
31330239.model_description: Fractional anisotropy, axial diffusivity, and radial diffusivity images from diffusion tensor imaging, processed with tract-based spatial statistics, are used to train Gaussian process classifiers. The classifiers are trained to distinguish diagnostic groups (bipolar disorder, disruptive mood dysregulation disorder, healthy volunteers) by white matter microstructure, controlling for age and sex.
31330239.headline_result: Classifier could not discriminate BD from DMDD; achieved 68% accuracy for DMDD vs. healthy volunteers and 75% accuracy for BD vs. healthy volunteers

31393626.clinical_problem: predicting vagus nerve stimulation response in children with drug-resistant epilepsy from structural and functional connectomic profiling
31393626.patient_population: 56 children with medically intractable epilepsy from 3 institutions (discovery n=38, validation n=18)
31393626.model_description: Diffusion tensor imaging identifies white matter microstructural differences between VNS responders and non-responders, which inform beamforming of resting-state magnetoencephalography functional connectivity. These structural and functional connectomic features are combined in a support vector machine trained to predict VNS response and independently validated in a separate cohort, outperforming a classifier built from clinical covariates alone.
31393626.headline_result: 89.5% accuracy, AUC 0.93 on 10-fold cross-validation; 83.3% accuracy (85.7% sensitivity, 75.0% specificity) in external validation; superior to clinical covariates alone (AUC 0.57, p < 0.008)
31393626.study_design: retrospective multi-institutional prognostic accuracy study with external validation

31827430.model_family: autoencoder jointly trained with a single-layer perceptron classifier
31827430.clinical_problem: classifying autism spectrum disorder from resting-state fMRI
31827430.patient_population: 1,035 subjects from the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE), across 17 imaging centers
31827430.model_description: ASD-DiagNet takes resting-state fMRI connectivity features and jointly trains an autoencoder with a single-layer-perceptron classifier to distinguish individuals with autism spectrum disorder from healthy controls. A linear-interpolation data-augmentation strategy generates synthetic training examples, and the method was evaluated on the public ABIDE dataset (1,035 subjects, 17 imaging centers). Code and trained model are released publicly.
31827430.release_evidence: "The implemented code is available as GPL license on GitHub portal of our lab (https://github.com/pcdslab/ASD-DiagNet)"
31827430.headline_result: Up to 28% increase in classification accuracy over prior state-of-the-art methods, maximum accuracy 82%, and much faster runtime (40 min vs. 7 h)
31827430.study_design: retrospective multi-site classification study using a public dataset

32114120.clinical_problem: estimating inattention and impulsivity severity scores in ADHD from resting-state fMRI dynamic connectivity
32114120.patient_population: 95 children with ADHD and 105 healthy controls from the ADHD-200 database
32114120.model_description: Dynamic features of intrinsic connectivity networks from resting-state fMRI, together with head-motion and other measures, are input to support vector regression models. The models estimate individual clinical scores of inattention and impulsivity in children with and without ADHD, with the sensorimotor network most associated with inattention and the executive control network with impulsivity.
32114120.dataset_size: 95 children with ADHD, 105 healthy controls (ADHD-200 database)
32114120.headline_result: Estimated scores correlated significantly with inattention (r = 0.4 ± 0.02, p < 0.01) and impulsivity (r = 0.31 ± 0.02, p < 0.01)

32634596.clinical_problem: predicting individual identity, IQ, and developmental quotient from structural brain connectome fingerprints
32634596.patient_population: individuals spanning toddlers to middle-aged adults; exact pediatric sample size not stated
32634596.model_description: A dynamic connectome modeling approach identifies a critical set of white matter subnetworks that serve as a personalized structural brain fingerprint. This fingerprint is used to identify individuals and to predict IQ in middle-aged adults and developmental quotient in toddlers, assessed for accuracy and reproducibility across the lifespan.
32634596.study_design: cross-sectional lifespan cohort study, technical development

32841716.clinical_problem: identifying morphological sex differences from structural MRI in pre-adolescent children
32841716.patient_population: 8,144 children, ages 9-10 years (Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study)
32841716.model_description: Minimally processed structural MRI scans from 8,144 pre-adolescent participants (ages 9-10) in the ABCD study are input to a data-driven deep learning model that identifies morphological brain structures distinguishing sex, accounting for head size, age, puberty, and socioeconomic status. The model highlighted cerebellar and subcortical structures, and a single summary score derived from the model predicted sex and correlated with working-memory-related cognitive performance.

33271266.model_family: shared response modeling (machine learning functional alignment)
33271266.clinical_problem: evaluating maturity and localization of adult-like brain functions in children using task fMRI functional alignment
33271266.patient_population: children ages 3-12 years watching a movie during fMRI; exact N not stated
33271266.model_description: A machine learning method called shared response modeling learns a lower-dimensional feature space from adult fMRI activity recorded while watching a movie. These learned features are translated into each child's individual anatomical brain space (ages 3-12) and used to reconstruct predicted activity, which is correlated with the child's actual fMRI activity to quantify the maturity and localization of adult-like brain functions across childhood.
33271266.headline_result: Reconstructed activity correlated reliably with children's actual fMRI activity throughout cortex; correlation strength in precuneus, inferior frontal gyrus, and lateral occipital cortex predicted chronological age
33271266.study_design: cross-sectional developmental fMRI study, technical development

33479511.clinical_problem: predicting irritability severity in youth from task fMRI functional connectivity during frustration
33479511.patient_population: 69 youths (mean age 14.55 years) with varying irritability across DMDD, ADHD, anxiety disorder, and control groups
33479511.model_description: Functional connectivity measured during a frustrating cognitive-flexibility fMRI task is input to connectome-based predictive modeling, a machine learning approach with 10-fold cross-validation. The model predicts child- and parent-reported irritability scores across a transdiagnostic sample of 69 youths, identifying predictive networks spanning motor-sensory, subcortical, salience, frontoparietal, and medial frontal regions.
33479511.headline_result: Connectivity during frustration predicted child-reported irritability (rho = 0.24, RMSE = 2.02, p = 0.03, permutation testing)

33771727.study_design: moderation/regression analysis of resting-state connectivity and behavior

34358659.study_design: cross-sectional diffusion tensor imaging with hierarchical cluster analysis

34823023.model_family: graph autoencoder, nonlinear latent factor deep learning model
34823023.clinical_problem: modeling brain structural connectome variation and its relationship to cognition
34823023.patient_population: children/adolescents from the ABCD study and adults from the Human Connectome Project
34823023.model_description: GATE is a nonlinear latent factor deep learning model that learns a low-dimensional representation of structural brain connectome graphs, where nodes are regions of interest and edges are connection strengths. Applied to the ABCD study and the Human Connectome Project, it characterizes the population distribution of brain networks and relates the learned representations to cognitive traits, outperforming prior topological-feature and PCA-based approaches.
34823023.dataset_size: not stated precisely (ABCD and Human Connectome Project cohorts)
34823023.headline_result: GATE showed large advantages over competing methods in prediction accuracy, statistical inference, and computing efficiency; structural connectome showed a stronger association with cognitive traits than prior approaches
34823023.study_design: methodological development with cross-sectional cohort application

35410904.study_design: retrospective MEG partial least-squares association study

35641152.clinical_problem: predicting fetal sex from prenatal resting-state fMRI functional connectivity
35641152.patient_population: 110 fetal resting-state fMRI scans from 95 fetuses, 19-40 gestational weeks
35641152.model_description: Resting-state fMRI functional connectivity patterns from fetuses (19-40 gestational weeks) are used to train multiple support vector machine models to classify fetal sex. The models identified consistent connections, particularly involving somatomotor, frontal, hippocampal, cerebellar, and basal ganglia regions, that reliably distinguished male from female fetuses before birth.
35641152.headline_result: SVM classified fetal sex with 73% accuracy from functional connectivity patterns

35751994.clinical_problem: predicting chronological age from resting-state functional connectivity in infants and toddlers
35751994.patient_population: 170 infants and toddlers, 8-26 months old (Baby Connectome Project)
35751994.model_description: Resting-state fMRI functional connectivity from infants and toddlers (8-26 months) in the Baby Connectome Project is used to derive individual connectome fingerprints and to train support vector regression models predicting age at scan. Connections were grouped into data-driven infant-specific functional networks; within-network connections predicted age significantly better than between-network connections.
35751994.headline_result: Models predicted novel infants' age within ±3.6 months error, prediction R2 = 0.51

36573438.clinical_problem: predicting sustained attention performance from functional connectivity in neurodiverse youth, including autism
36573438.patient_population: youth including participants with autism spectrum disorder and neurotypical participants, across 5 datasets
36573438.model_description: Functional connectome data from youth performing an in-scan sustained attention task, including participants with neurodiverse conditions such as autism, are used to train connectome-based predictive models. The model developed in one dataset was validated in a separate neurotypical sample performing the same task, and its stability across months to years was examined via connectome-based identification in three additional longitudinal datasets.
36573438.headline_result: Successful prediction of in-scan sustained attention performance in the primary sample; the attention network model generalized to predict attention in an independent neurotypical sample
36573438.study_design: multi-dataset cross-sectional and longitudinal cohort study

36603025.model_family: multivariate machine learning decoding (within- and between-format)
36603025.clinical_problem: decoding cortical representations of numerals and nonsymbolic quantity in children
36603025.patient_population: 89 children, either at the beginning of formal schooling (age 5) or four years in (age 8)
36603025.model_description: Multivariate fMRI adaptation data are combined with within- and between-format machine learning decoding to probe cortical representations of Arabic numerals and approximate nonsymbolic quantity in 89 children aged 5 or 8 years. The decoding approach tests whether the same neural code represents numerals and nonsymbolic quantities, finding a format-independent representation in right parietal cortex only in 5-year-olds.
36603025.headline_result: Format-independent neural representation of quantity found in right parietal cortex, present only in 5-year-olds

38217837.study_design: cross-sectional diffusion tensor imaging with hierarchical cluster analysis

39251706.clinical_problem: predicting socioeconomic environment (household income and neighborhood education) from adolescent brain connectome data
39251706.patient_population: 9,099 children/adolescents from the ABCD study, United States
39251706.model_description: Brain connectome data from 9,099 adolescents in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study are input to a linear support vector machine trained to classify each adolescent's socioeconomic environment (household income and neighborhood education, dichotomized at various percentile thresholds), using brain connectivity alone.
39251706.headline_result: Best classification performance (20th/80th percentile thresholds, household income plus neighborhood education) achieved AUPRC of 0.8224; 8 significant predictive connections identified in parietal and frontal lobes

39592647.clinical_problem: predicting postmenstrual/brain age from structural and functional connectomes in preterm and term neonates
39592647.patient_population: 611 infants (174 preterm, 437 term) in the first month of life (Developing Human Connectome Project)
39592647.model_description: Resting-state fMRI and diffusion tensor imaging data from 611 neonates (term and preterm) in the Developing Human Connectome Project are used to build structural and functional connectomes. Connectome-based predictive modeling, a machine learning approach, is trained to estimate postmenstrual age from these connectomes; the gap between predicted and chronological age is then related to perinatal exposures and toddler behavioral outcomes.
39592647.headline_result: Structural and functional connectomes accurately predicted postmenstrual age for both term and preterm infants; brain age gaps were associated with perinatal exposures and toddler behavioral outcomes

39877891.clinical_problem: predicting future BMI and food-approach behavior in children with obesity from hippocampal effective connectivity
39877891.patient_population: 39 children with overweight/obesity and 51 children with normal weight, ages 8-12 years, with 1-year follow-up
39877891.model_description: Resting-state fMRI functional and effective connectivity (via spectral dynamic causal modeling) of the hippocampus are measured in children aged 8-12 with and without excess weight. Linear support vector regression is trained on baseline hippocampal connectivity to predict BMI and food-approach eating behavior measured one year later, identifying altered bidirectional hippocampus-postcentral gyrus connectivity as predictive.
39877891.headline_result: Altered bidirectional hippocampus-postcentral gyrus effective connectivity predicted BMI and food-approach behavior one year later

39997997.model_family: graph neural networks (simple and residual graph convolutional networks), compared with multi-layer perceptron, random forest, and SVM
39997997.clinical_problem: sex classification from pediatric and adult structural brain connectome data
39997997.patient_population: adult BRIGHT dataset (147 Hodgkin lymphoma survivors, 162 age-matched controls) and pediatric HCP-Development dataset (135 healthy subjects)
39997997.model_description: Structural brain connectome graphs (nodes as brain regions, edges as white matter connection strength) from adult and pediatric datasets are input to graph neural network models (simple and residual graph convolutional networks), compared against a multilayer perceptron, random forest, and support vector machine. Architecture experiments test network depth, pooling, and skip connections, with performance assessed by accuracy, AUC, and adversarial robustness; adult-trained models were also extended to and augmented with pediatric data.
39997997.headline_result: Adult GNN models achieved 85.1% accuracy in sex classification on unseen adult participants; the best model using pediatric data augmentation achieved 83.0% accuracy on pediatric and 81.3% on adult participants
39997997.study_design: retrospective multi-cohort methodological and classification study

40222403.body_region: brain (subcortical regions: amygdala, hippocampus, nucleus accumbens)
40222403.clinical_problem: assessing effects of perceived racial discrimination on longitudinal subcortical functional connectivity changes and internalizing/externalizing symptoms in adolescents
40222403.patient_population: 3,321 racial/ethnic minority youth from the ABCD study, split into training (n=2,674) and testing (n=647) sets
40222403.model_description: Resting-state fMRI functional connectivity of the nucleus accumbens, amygdala, and hippocampus is measured at baseline and two years later in adolescents from the ABCD study. Propensity score-weighted machine learning, trained and cross-validated on 80% of the sample and independently tested on the remaining 20%, assesses the effect of perceived discrimination on 2-year connectivity changes, followed by mediation analyses linking these brain changes to internalizing and externalizing symptoms.
40222403.headline_result: Perceived discrimination was significantly associated with 2-year connectivity changes in nucleus accumbens, amygdala, and hippocampus in both cross-validation and independent testing

40224616.clinical_problem: distinguishing pediatric PTSD from trauma-exposed non-PTSD controls using diffusion tensor imaging white matter microstructure
40224616.patient_population: 48 participants under age 18: 24 treatment-naive PTSD patients and 24 trauma-exposed non-PTSD controls, matched for age, sex, and education
40224616.model_description: Diffusion tensor imaging metrics (fractional anisotropy, axial and radial diffusivity) along major white matter tracts are measured in treatment-naive pediatric PTSD patients and trauma-exposed non-PTSD controls under age 18. Support vector machine analyses are trained to distinguish PTSD from non-PTSD using pointwise microstructural measurements, with axial diffusivity providing the best classification performance.
40224616.dataset_size: 48 participants under 18 (24 PTSD, 24 trauma-exposed non-PTSD controls)
40224616.headline_result: Pointwise axial diffusivity measurements gave the best PTSD vs. trauma-exposed non-PTSD classification performance; white matter abnormalities correlated with PTSD symptom severity

40567457.clinical_problem: predicting preadolescent irritability severity from whole-brain task fMRI during reward anticipation
40567457.model_description: Whole-brain fMRI activity acquired during the reward-anticipation period of a monetary incentive delay task in 6,065 preadolescents from the ABCD study is input directly to a 3D convolutional neural network trained to predict parent-reported irritability severity as a continuous score. Regression activation mapping identifies brain regions, including the caudate, amygdala, parahippocampal gyrus, and hippocampus, most predictive of irritability.
40567457.headline_result: Mean squared error 1.82; mean absolute error 0.48 ± 1.54 SD predicting irritability severity scores
40567457.study_design: cross-sectional multi-site cohort study, technical development

40654936.model_family: deep learning model using structural MRI brain measures
40654936.clinical_problem: predicting current and future internalizing problems (anxiety and depression) in youth from structural brain MRI
40654936.patient_population: youth from four large-scale datasets: ABCD, Healthy Brain Network, HCP-Development, and Province of Ontario Neurodevelopmental network (N=14,523 cross-sectional; N=10,540 longitudinal)
40654936.model_description: Structural MRI measures of cortical thickness, surface area, and volume from four large pediatric neuroimaging datasets are input to deep learning models. One model predicts clinically significant internalizing problems cross-sectionally, and another predicts subsequent worsening of internalizing symptoms longitudinally, using stratified cross-validation and testing in independent held-out and external samples.
40654936.release_evidence: Preprint (bioRxiv); no repository or product named, per RECHECK rule for preprints
40654936.headline_result: Cross-sectional model AUC 0.80 [95% CI 0.71-0.88]; longitudinal model AUC 0.66 [0.65-0.67] in the general population, AUC 0.80 [0.78-0.81] in an external test set of primarily neurodevelopmental conditions, AUC 0.73 [0.70-0.76] across all neurodevelopmental conditions
40654936.study_design: cross-sectional and longitudinal multi-dataset cohort study, preprint

40657594.model_family: LASSO (least absolute shrinkage and selection operator) regression
40657594.clinical_problem: predicting adolescent anhedonia from demographic, clinical, and task fMRI reward-related neural factors
40657594.patient_population: 73 adolescents, ages 13-19 years, at varying familial risk for anhedonia
40657594.model_description: Demographic and clinical characteristics along with task fMRI activation and functional connectivity measured during a monetary reward paradigm are combined as candidate predictors for LASSO regression, a feature-selection machine learning method, in 73 adolescents followed for up to two years. The model selects 10 features, including impulsivity, dorsal caudate/temporal/cuneus activation, and ventral striatum connectivity, that predict peak anhedonia severity over the follow-up period.
40657594.headline_result: 10 selected features (including impulsivity and reward-network connectivity) predicted peak anhedonia over two years; neural factors explained an additional 40% of variance beyond impulsivity alone

40764552.model_family: XGBoost classifier with AI Fairness 360 bias-mitigation/reweighing algorithms
40764552.clinical_problem: gender-debiased ADHD diagnosis from clinical and neuroimaging (functional and structural MRI) features
40764552.patient_population: 400 children and adolescents with and without ADHD (98 females: 25 ADHD, 73 typically developing), a subsample of the Child Mind Institute dataset
40764552.model_description: Personal characteristics, Child Behavior Checklist scores, and neuroimaging features (fMRI wavelet variance coefficients in one dataset, structural MRI radiomic features in another) from 400 children and adolescents train ADHD diagnostic classifiers. Multiple bias-mitigation algorithms from the AI Fairness 360 toolbox reduce a previously reported gender disparity in ADHD diagnosis; a reweighed XGBoost model achieved the best accuracy and fairness, tested on an independently acquired test set from an earlier study.
40764552.dataset_size: 400 children and adolescents (98 females: 25 ADHD, 73 typically developing)
40764552.headline_result: Reweighed XGBoost model achieved the best accuracy and highest fairness among tested bias-mitigation approaches on both fMRI and structural MRI datasets
40764552.study_design: retrospective classification study with an external test set

40822420.study_design: prospective infant cohort regression study with replication sample

40858546.model_family: adversarial deep canonical correlation analysis deep learning model
40858546.clinical_problem: identifying ADHD-specific gene-white matter microstructure associations using diffusion tensor imaging and genotype data
40858546.patient_population: 600 Chinese children with ADHD and typically developing controls
40858546.model_description: Diffusion tensor imaging white matter microstructure measures and genotype data from 600 Chinese children with and without ADHD are input to an adversarial deep canonical correlation analysis model (A-DCCA), a deep learning method designed to separate ADHD-specific from shared gene-white-matter association patterns. Interpretable deep learning analysis then identifies which white matter regions and genes contribute to ADHD-specific versus non-specific associations.
40858546.dataset_size: 600 children (ADHD and typically developing), Chinese cohort
40858546.study_design: cross-sectional case-control cohort study, technical development

40883286.model_family: deep learning model using structural MRI brain measures
40883286.clinical_problem: predicting current and future internalizing problems (anxiety and depression) in youth from structural brain MRI
40883286.patient_population: youth from four large-scale datasets: ABCD, Healthy Brain Network, HCP-Development, and Province of Ontario Neurodevelopmental network (N=14,523 cross-sectional; N=10,540 longitudinal)
40883286.model_description: Structural MRI measures of cortical thickness, surface area, and volume from four large pediatric neuroimaging datasets are input to deep learning models. One model predicts clinically significant internalizing problems cross-sectionally, and another predicts subsequent worsening of internalizing symptoms longitudinally, using stratified cross-validation and testing in independent held-out and external samples.
40883286.headline_result: Cross-sectional model AUC 0.80 [95% CI 0.71-0.88]; longitudinal model AUC 0.66 [0.65-0.67] in the general population, AUC 0.80 [0.78-0.81] in an external test set of primarily neurodevelopmental conditions, AUC 0.73 [0.70-0.76] across all neurodevelopmental conditions
40883286.study_design: cross-sectional and longitudinal multi-dataset cohort study

40949947.model_family: dynamic resting-state fMRI predictive models (published adult model, linear DMN/connectome models, exploratory random forest)
40949947.clinical_problem: predicting adolescent rumination severity from dynamic resting-state fMRI connectivity
40949947.model_description: Dynamic resting-state fMRI connectivity, including default-mode network connections, is used with several predictive models, an adult-derived dynamic connectivity model, linear default-mode-network and whole-brain connectome models, and an exploratory random forest, to predict self-reported trait rumination in the largest adolescent sample studied to date (n=443). None of these models generalized well to held-out or external adolescent data.
40949947.release_evidence: Preprint (bioRxiv); no repository or product named, per RECHECK rule for preprints
40949947.headline_result: The adult dynamic connectivity model failed to generalize; linear DMN and whole-brain connectome models failed to generalize to held-out data; an exploratory random forest model did not generalize to an external sample with a distinct scanner protocol

41000961.clinical_problem: predicting developmental language trajectories from infant resting-state fMRI language-network connectivity
41000961.patient_population: infants from the Baby Connectome Project, followed across the first year of life
41000961.model_description: Resting-state fMRI data from infants in the Baby Connectome Project are used to measure functional connectivity of language-related brain regions across the first year of life. A data-driven machine learning algorithm partitions infants into three groups (Delayed, Typical, and Advanced) by language-development trajectory, and connectivity differences among these groups predict later language outcome scores measured at two years.
41000961.release_evidence: Preprint (bioRxiv); no repository or product named, per RECHECK rule for preprints
41000961.dataset_size: not stated precisely (Baby Connectome Project infants, first year of life)
41000961.headline_result: Magnitude of connectivity differences consistently predicted later language scores at two-year outcome across several language assessments
41000961.study_design: prospective longitudinal infant cohort study, preprint

41002215.study_design: task fMRI study using natural language processing of verbal responses, correlational analysis

41176878.study_design: whole-brain task fMRI activation and connectivity analysis
